description: Let’s Solve Big Problems! I’m Marvelous Adeola Ajao, Computer Engineer & 2025 NASA Space Apps participant. Seeking Frontend Devs (Svelte/JS), Backend Engineers (Laravel), UI/UX Designers, and creative problem-solvers. Let’s build something meaningful together. Join me to turn tough NASA challenges into elegant, user-friendly solutions.
summary:
Star Detective is a web-based astronomy academy that takes anyone from zero to examining real images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission in five stages.
Learners start with Baby Steps, which covers key terms such as infrared, comet and glitch. Next, Known Findings shows how objects like Pluto were found by comparing photos taken at different times. The Solar System explains why nearby objects appear to move against distant stars. In Training, learners flip between aligned SPHEREx images of the same patch of sky, decide whether something moved, and learn to tell real objects from camera glitches. In Explore, they compare SPHEREx images from different dates on their own, using blink and swipe views.
Our Python pipeline downloads cutouts from NASA’s IRSA archive, aligns them, and matches their wavelengths, so stars stay fixed and real changes stand out.
SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, which is more data than any team can inspect by eye. Star Detective turns that archive into something the public can understand and use. Software prepares the images, and people make the call.
details:
Star Detective: Spot What Moved in the SPHEREx Sky

What it does and how it works

Star Detective is a web app that teaches people to search real NASA SPHEREx infrared images for moving objects, the same way astronomers have hunted for new worlds since Uranus in 1781. It answers the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge directly. You enter a sky position (RA/Dec), and the tool pulls SPHEREx images of that patch from NASA/IPAC's public IRSA archive. It plays them back as a flip-book so anything that moved stands out.

Learners progress through a five-stage Academy:

1. Basics. Infrared light, false colour, what SPHEREx is, and why stars look "fixed" while comets, asteroids and brown dwarfs move.

2. History of discovery. Uranus, Ceres, Barnard's Star, Pluto, WISE 0855, Comet 3I/ATLAS and the Planet Nine hypothesis.

3. Our Solar System in context.

4. Quick Spotter (training). Players blink between two images of the same sky and click the object that moved. The server checks the click. It awards XP, flags it if the player picked a one-frame cosmic-ray glitch, and shows a reveal card about the real object (for example WISE 0855, Barnard's Star or Luhman 16).

5. Explore. Open-ended viewing of real SPHEREx data. Users can log unusual signals as candidates, clearly labelled as needing further checks rather than called discoveries.

Behind the scenes, the backend finds SPHEREx exposures through IVOA SIA/TAP queries, downloads small server-side cutouts, and groups them into observation epochs. It subtracts the zodiacal-light model and background, then reprojects every frame onto one shared north-up grid with one shared brightness stretch. That way, apparent motion between frames is real motion and not a processing artifact.

Benefits

• Opens up a brand-new NASA dataset to students and the public without asking them to learn FITS files or astronomy software.

• Teaches real scientific habits: comparing epochs, telling a moving object from a detector glitch, and keeping "candidate" separate from "discovery."

• Every image is labelled as Real or Simulated and shows its observation date, so users always know what they are looking at.

• A "Dual-Vision" toggle switches between vivid false colour for beginners and raw monochrome for people who want the authentic data.

Intended impact

We want people to try citizen science, not just watch it. Moving-object searches have found new worlds for centuries, and SPHEREx now maps the whole sky in infrared every six months. Star Detective turns that archive into a guided path from "what is infrared?" to examining real data and flagging candidates. We hope it builds both curiosity and scientific honesty in students, educators and space fans, and gets more eyes on SPHEREx data.

Tools, languages and software

• Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Next.js 16, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Base UI, Three.js (3D solar system and asteroid models), GSAP and Framer Motion (animation), and react-compare-slider (image comparison).

• Backend: Python with FastAPI and Pydantic, plus Astropy, reproject, NumPy, Matplotlib and Pillow for loading, aligning and rendering FITS images.

• Data: the NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx archive, accessed through the IVOA SIA v2 and TAP protocols. Imagery credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech, ESA, STScI and NASA 3D Resources.

• Infrastructure: PostgreSQL (user accounts, XP and leaderboard), JWT/Argon2 authentication, Render (API and database), Vercel (frontend), Git/GitHub.

• Hardware: standard laptops only. All data comes from NASA's public archives.

What makes it creative

• It turns a centuries-old technique, blink comparison, into a game while keeping the real science intact.

• The difficulty ramps up gradually: lessons, then history, then guided training with known answers, then open exploration of real, unlabelled sky.

• Glitches are part of the game. Clicking a cosmic-ray hit is a teaching moment, not just a wrong answer, which is exactly the mistake real observers have to learn to avoid.

• The pipeline is ready for future data. When NASA publishes a new SPHEREx data release, the app can use it with a configuration change and no code changes.

Factors the team considered

• Scientific honesty. We never invent data. If the archive can't be reached and nothing is cached, the app says so. Simulated targets are disclosed, and the app never claims to find Planet X.

• Accuracy. Frames are properly aligned and use the same brightness stretch so that motion is real. Historical facts were checked against NASA and IAU sources.

• Accessibility and approachability. No astronomy background is needed. The app has plain-language definitions, works on phones (click coordinates are normalized for mobile), and offers false-colour and raw views.

• Reliability. Cutouts are cached so repeat visits load fast and work offline. If the backend is down, users can still play a bundled level.

• Credit and licensing. Every image and 3D asset is attributed, with links to its source.

• Cost and deployment. The app runs on free hosting tiers so anyone can use it.
